standfirst: Two young boxers take a part-time job with a loan shark and spend the rest of the series regretting it. Season one is the one that works, and the reason is the friendship: a genuine two-man powerhouse, filmed by people who cared more about choreography than about plot. This page is for that season. Season two, which finished airing in April 2026, is reviewed on its own page, because it is a different and worse proposition: better fights, slack plotting, and a hero who cries more than he fights.

picks.why: The best-made show in this whole neighbourhood. Violence with weight and consequence, fights shot so you can read every exchange, and a friendship that carries the entire eight episodes. If the brotherhood in season one was the reason you watched, this does that better than Bloodhounds ever manages. Difference: it is genuinely upsetting rather than fun. There is no swagger and no winning, and the ending offers no relief.

The same shape for the same reason: two young men, one calm and one loud, whose friendship is the actual subject. Same conscription-era masculinity, same interest in what predatory power does to people with no leverage. Difference: there is nobody to fight. It is a procedural about hazing and paperwork, and it is much heavier and much sadder.

For the appetite to see predatory money dismantled with style. An outsider with resources, a building full of people worth defending, and a villain the show is happy to make you enjoy hating. Difference: it is a black comedy with cartoon logic and a lawyer's mind, so the physical stakes never feel real the way a Bloodhounds fight does.

Revenge with a body cost, in eight episodes and no filler. Somebody trained, sent inside an organisation, and visibly damaged by it, with hand-to-hand work that is among the best Korea has put on Netflix. Difference: no friendship and no comedy, and it is considerably bleaker. Nobody is saved by loyalty here.

If you were mostly there for people who deserve it getting what is coming. Victims the system ignored, an episodic revenge outfit, and a satisfying beating on a reliable schedule. Difference: pulp with a case-of-the-week rhythm, no season-long villain and no real jeopardy for anyone you like.

Righteous violence played for laughs. A priest with a temper, a corrupt local power structure, and fight scenes staged as comedy without ever being weightless. Difference: it is a broad comedy first, forty episodes long in its original cut, and nothing in it will make you tense.

against.title: Sweet Home
against.why: The other loud Korean Netflix action show with a young male lead, which is the only reason it turns up here. It is creature horror set in an apartment block, driven by monster design and body horror. Bloodhounds is about two people who are very good at hitting. No overlap beyond the platform.

against.title: Vagabond
against.why: Paired for the action, and the action is genuinely good. But it is a sixteen-episode espionage conspiracy that spends most of its runtime on plot it never resolves. Bloodhounds is eight lean episodes with a fist at the centre of every one. The bloat is the whole difference.

against.title: Bad and Crazy
against.why: The other buddy-action series where the pairing is the point. Its hook is a psychological premise about what one of the two men actually is, and the tone swings hard between comedy and darkness. If you wanted more boxing and more brotherhood, the gimmick will get in the way.
